title: What to write down in case something happens to you
dek: Create a short handover with contacts, essential commitments and document locations, while keeping private access details and legal authority separate.
metaDescription: Create a short handover with contacts, essential commitments and document locations, while keeping private access details and legal authority separate.

paragraphs: Write down who to contact, who depends on you, which commitments need attention and where the important records are. Keep this first page an index, not a bundle of passwords or full account numbers. Tell a trusted person where to find it and what help you are asking for.

Imagine being temporarily unable to answer messages. A friend may know you well but not know who collects a child, which household payment is approaching or where your insurance papers are. This guide makes that first handover easier. It is not a will, an advance directive or permission to use your accounts.

body.heading: Start with the next few days
paragraphs: Ask what would become difficult if you were unreachable tomorrow. For some households that is a care arrangement; for others it is access to the home or an employer who expects a reply. List the immediate continuity jobs before trying to catalog everything you own.

Write the contact's role as well as their name. 'Ask Alex to notify work' is different from 'Alex has authority over my money.' If a person has a formal appointment, point to the document and record where the current version is kept. Do not assume the title emergency contact grants decision-making power.

body.heading: Make the short handover
items: Name a first contact and willing backup, with current ways to reach them.
List dependants and the location of their established care instructions.
Identify urgent household commitments and where the current bills or calendar can be found.
List important providers by name, not every private account identifier.
Record where legal, identity and insurance documents are kept and who can lawfully obtain them.
Point to a protected digital-access plan or provider legacy setting rather than exposing secrets here.
Date the page and tell the intended helper where it is.

body.heading: Invented example: enough detail to start
rows: Ask Jo first; backup is Mina. Contact details in the private contact list.
Dependent's care plan is in the labeled home folder; contact the existing care team.
See current household bills list, including housing and insurance.
Current legal originals kept with the named adviser; copies in the protected folder.
Provider-specific plan and recovery instructions are stored separately.

body.heading: Use two levels of privacy
paragraphs: The first page can contain names and locations, but those are still personal information. Share it only with people who need it and choose storage appropriate to your situation. A note pointing to a safe is not harmless if it also explains exactly how to open it.

Keep sensitive identifiers, passwords, recovery codes, access keys and medical detail in a more protected arrangement. There is no need to make the same page both easy to find and capable of opening every account. Your trusted person should know the lawful route to the next record, not receive unrestricted access by accident.

body.heading: Do not turn access planning into impersonation
paragraphs: Knowing a phone passcode or having a physical key does not settle whether someone may transact, read private material or make decisions. Check each institution's process and any relevant legal arrangements. For money or healthcare authority, obtain appropriate advice rather than relying on a note saying 'please handle everything.'

For your own Google account, [Inactive Account Manager](https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/3036546?hl=en) allows chosen data sharing or notification after a selected period of inactivity. It is not an immediate emergency login and does not provide unrestricted access. Other providers need their own current checks.

body.heading: Test the locations rather than sharing secrets
paragraphs: Ask your intended helper, while you are available, to locate the page and explain which contact they would approach first. Have them identify an unclear location such as 'office file.' You can correct it to a useful description without showing private document contents.

Test practical barriers too. Is the folder in a locked home nobody can enter? Does the backup know they were named? Is the only copy on a device that requires you to unlock it? Solve the retrieval problem with the right level of privacy rather than hiding the record more thoroughly.

body.heading: Ask a person before naming them

items.line: Would you be willing to be the first contact if I cannot respond? I am writing a short list of who to call and where the important records are.
This page does not give you authority over accounts or medical decisions. It should help you find the right people and documents.
Can you find the page and tell me which instruction is unclear? You do not need to read the private records it points to.

body.heading: When a page is not enough
paragraphs: Children, a business, care responsibilities, disputed relationships or property in several places may need more detailed arrangements. The [NIA affairs-in-order checklist](https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/advance-care-planning/getting-your-affairs-order-checklist-documents-prepare-future?page=1) is an official planning starting point; this revision reviewed its search listing, not the blocked full page. Use qualified legal or care professionals for documents that establish authority.

If there is coercion, abuse or a risk that a person will misuse access, do not hand over a comprehensive map of your affairs to them. Seek confidential professional help to plan access and contacts safely. Trust and convenience are not the only considerations.

body.heading: Keep it current without rewriting your life
paragraphs: Review after changes in contacts, home, work, care or providers, and choose a periodic reminder that you can maintain. Mark the last review date. Remove obsolete shared copies where possible and tell helpers when the location changes.

When the first page works, expand using [the fuller if-something-happens file](/guides/the-if-something-happens-to-me-file). Keep this page short enough to answer the first few questions, rather than duplicating the whole archive. Unknown entries can become a small follow-up list.

items.q: Is this the same as a will?
items.a: No. This page is a practical index to people, commitments and records. Legal documents have their own purposes and validity rules. A useful location note does not create financial authority, appoint a guardian or replace instructions for medical decisions.

items.q: Should the helper have my passwords?
items.a: Use a protected, provider-appropriate access plan rather than putting passwords on the first page. Consider authorization as well as technical access. The right arrangement depends on the provider and situation; a recovery feature may share limited data or require a separate request.

items.q: What if I cannot finish every line?
items.a: Finish the useful parts and mark unknowns. Prioritize the first contact, immediate dependants and document location. A partial page should be labeled honestly so nobody assumes a blank means nothing exists. Give each consequential gap a next action rather than inventing an answer.
